text:
I've drafted the section below. It's organized around the main tension in the field (algorithm aversion vs. algorithm appreciation) and then the factors researchers have proposed to explain it. Every citation is to a paper I found and read the abstract of. Because I worked only from abstracts, please check specific claims against the full papers before you submit.

---

## 2. Related Work

### 2.1 Algorithms outperform people, but people don't always use them

The debate starts with the "clinical versus actuarial" literature. Across many domains, formal statistical prediction matches or beats unaided human judgment. A meta-analysis of studies on human health and behavior found mechanical prediction was about 10% more accurate on average. It substantially outperformed clinical prediction in 33–47% of studies, and clinicians were substantially better in only 6–16% [W2168729696]. This advantage held regardless of the task, the type of judge, or the judges' experience [W2168729696]. Even so, decision makers in applied settings have been slow to adopt such aids. In employee selection, for example, the reluctance has been traced to implicit beliefs that favor intuition and subjective judgment [W2171321543].

### 2.2 Algorithm aversion

Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey named this pattern *algorithm aversion*. In five incentivized studies, people who watched an algorithm make forecasts became less confident in it and less likely to bet on it over an inferior human, even when they had seen it outperform the human. The reason was that people lost confidence in algorithms faster than in humans after seeing the same mistake [W3125633690]. Later work supports the idea that errors are judged asymmetrically. After bad advice, people used automated advice much less, while their use of human advice dropped far less [W2600700815]. Erring algorithms also draw harsher gut reactions and less forgiveness than erring humans, and this held regardless of the algorithm's maturity, the severity of the error, or the domain [W3167050492]. A longitudinal field study (18 days of financial forecasting) found that inaccurate algorithms were penalized more than equally inaccurate humans, though the penalty faded over time [W4206941179].

Other explanations go beyond reactions to errors. Dietvorst and Bharti show that people have *diminishing sensitivity to forecasting error*. They prefer riskier, higher-variance methods such as human judgment in uncertain domains because those methods seem more likely to produce a near-perfect answer [W2974452734]. In medicine, Longoni, Bonezzi and Morewedge identify *uniqueness neglect*: the belief that AI cannot account for a person's unique circumstances. It drives resistance to AI care and is stronger among people who see themselves as unique [W2942858056]. In moral domains, people object to algorithms partly because they assume algorithms make decisions by maximizing an outcome [W3181173654], and partly because they value humans' freedom to depart from fixed fairness rules [W4210390504]. Turel and Kalhan add an unconscious explanation: implicit prejudice against AI shapes early reliance, and its weight shrinks as people learn how the algorithm actually performs [W4391114267].

### 2.3 Algorithm appreciation

A second body of work challenges the idea that aversion is the default. In six experiments, Logg, Minson and Moore found that lay people followed advice *more* when they thought it came from an algorithm rather than a person. They called this *algorithm appreciation*, and it went against what researchers themselves had predicted [W2800068874]. Appreciation weakened in two cases: when people chose between the algorithm and their *own* judgment rather than another person's, and among experienced professional forecasters, who relied less on algorithms and were less accurate as a result [W2800068874]. Later studies have replicated appreciation within the judge-advisor paradigm. It was driven by higher trust in the algorithmic advisor and survived disclosure of the algorithm's errors in aggregate form [W4281822284]. People also rely more on algorithms, relative to the crowd's opinion, as intellective tasks get harder [W3152500611]. Prahl and Van Swol did not replicate a general preference for human advice in the first place [W2600700815]. In public-sector decisions, Alon-Barkat and Busuioc found no evidence of automation bias (overreliance on algorithmic advice) relative to equivalent human-expert advice. Instead, both algorithmic and human-expert advice were followed more when it matched stereotypes [W4211002924].

### 2.4 Reconciling the two: moderators

Several reviews and theory papers treat aversion and appreciation as outcomes that depend on conditions rather than as fixed traits. Burton, Stein and Jensen reviewed 61 articles and grouped the proposed causes and solutions into five themes: expectations and expertise, decision autonomy, incentives, cognitive compatibility, and divergent rationalities [W2981686111]. Mahmud et al. reviewed 80 empirical studies and grouped influencing factors as algorithm, individual, task, and high-level factors. They noted that task-level and high-level factors are understudied [W4200546216]. Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl argue that the field lacks a shared definition and way of measuring these constructs. They separate four *decision configurations* (evaluating algorithms, human advisors, one's own judgment, or combinations), and the direction of the effect partly depends on which configuration a study uses [W4400803056]. This fits Logg et al.'s finding that appreciation fades when people compare the algorithm with themselves [W2800068874]. Hou and Jung produced both appreciation and aversion just by changing how the human and algorithmic agents were described, with the effect mediated by perceived expertise [W3206874785]. That suggests differences in experimental framing may explain much of the disagreement between studies.

The moderators studied most often are:

- **Task type and subjectivity.** For "human" tasks that seem to need intuition or subjective judgment, algorithmic decisions are rated less fair and trustworthy. For mechanical tasks they are rated about the same as human decisions [W2792183666]. More difficult or complex tasks tend to increase reliance on algorithms [W3152500611], [W3193926864]. Inherent uncertainty in a domain reduces it [W2974452734].
- **Expertise and self-confidence.** Experts discount algorithmic advice [W2800068874]. A person's confidence in themselves, rather than in the AI, has been found to drive whether they accept AI suggestions [W3199747482].
- **Lay beliefs about AI.** People who believe AI exceeds human intelligence are more likely to take algorithmic advice, especially on complex tasks [W3193926864].
- **Stakes and moral relevance.** Morally relevant tradeoffs and moral discretion increase aversion [W3181173654], [W4210390504]. Uniqueness concerns matter in personal, high-stakes areas like medicine [W2942858056].

### 2.5 Interventions

Design interventions often target the proposed mechanisms. Letting users modify an algorithm's forecast, even slightly, makes them much more willing to use it, and this has been linked to a desire for *some* control [W3121705224]. A replication in a CHI paper only partly confirmed this "outcome control" effect. It found that "process control," such as choosing the training algorithm, also helps, but changing the input variables does not [W4366547314]. Because aversion often comes from the belief that algorithms cannot learn, showing that an algorithm learns from its mistakes reduces aversion [W4283162852], [W3110817755]. Effects of transparency are more mixed. Showing an algorithm that seems too *simple* hurts advice use [W3189444386], and detailed performance information can reduce appreciation by increasing cognitive load [W4281822284]. In medicine, framing AI as personalized, or as supporting rather than replacing a clinician, removes resistance [W2942858056].

### 2.6 Trust calibration and appropriate reliance

Human-factors research on automation offers a complementary view. The question there is whether reliance is *appropriate*, not whether people prefer algorithms. Lee and See's model describes how trust guides reliance when a system is too complex to understand fully. Trust forms through analytic, analogical and affective processes, and its appropriateness depends on context and on how the system's characteristics are displayed [W4243342770]. Glikson and Woolley's review of trust in AI distinguishes cognitive trust (shaped by tangibility, transparency, reliability and immediacy) from emotional trust (shaped by anthropomorphism). They also note that the evidence relies heavily on short-term lab studies [W3013998503]. This framing matters because both under-reliance (aversion) and over-reliance (e.g., following a poor AI because people blame themselves for errors [W3199747482]) are failures of calibration.

### 2.7 Gaps

Three gaps stand out:
1. Inconsistent definitions and measures make findings hard to compare [W4400803056], [W3206874785].
2. Task-level and contextual factors are underexplored compared with features of the algorithm and the individual [W4200546216].
3. Most studies are short-term lab experiments [W3013998503]. The few longitudinal studies suggest aversion changes over time [W4206941179], [W4391114267].

- **Classic papers I couldn't find in the database:** Meehl (1954), Dawes (1979), Parasuraman & Riley (1997, "misuse, disuse, abuse"), Castelo, Bos & Lehmann (2019, "Task-dependent algorithm aversion"), and Yeomans et al. - **Results that pull against the main story.** Prahl & Van Swol [W2600700815] and Alon-Barkat & Busuioc [W4211002924] report null or mixed effects. - **Possible additions:** systematic reviews I didn't use, such as [W3024435124], [W3042817621] and [W4385299043], and newer work on generative AI [W7127239690].

My study is an online experiment where people choose between advice from an algorithm and advice from a human expert, across tasks that range from forecasting to things that feel more subjective, like predicting which jokes or movies someone will like. text:
I've revised the related-work section around your design: a choice between an algorithm and a human expert, on tasks ranging from forecasting to taste prediction. The new searches turned up several papers that fit closely. Two of them use the same domains as your study: jokes [W2913854599] and movies [W2075329139]. There is also an older forecasting study that compares a human *expert* directly with a statistical method [W2158570360]. As before, I worked from abstracts only.

---

## 2. Related Work

### 2.1 Where the debate started: clinical versus statistical prediction

Whether to trust formulas or human judgment is a much older question than the term "algorithm aversion." It goes back to Meehl's 1954 book *Clinical versus Statistical Prediction*, which compared expert judgment with formal combinations of the same data [W2056418346], [W2129871510]. The roots go back further still. In 1928 Burgess built a parole-outcome predictor from 21 objective factors for about 3,000 Illinois parolees [W2102256472]. Over the following decades, the findings consistently favored the formula. Dawes argued that when a numerical outcome is predicted from numerical inputs, even *improper* linear models beat clinical intuition, including models whose weights are set by intuition or simply made equal [W2056418346]. Grove and Meehl reviewed 136 studies and concluded that the mechanical method is "almost invariably equal to or superior to" the clinical one [W2102256472]. A later meta-analysis put the average advantage at about 10%. Humans were substantially more accurate in only 6–16% of studies, and the result held regardless of the judges' experience [W2168729696]. Recent machine-learning work points the same way in high-stakes settings such as bail decisions [W2551317447]. In business forecasting, though, combining a model with managerial intuition beat either one on its own [W2104546629]. That suggests "algorithm versus human" is not always the right framing.

This literature also recorded people's **resistance** to formulas from the start. Reviews observed that actuarial methods were "rarely employed in practice" despite being more accurate [W207333959]. Dawes [W2056418346] and Grove and Meehl [W2102256472] discussed the technical, psychological and ethical objections people raise and tried to answer them. Similar beliefs favoring intuition were later shown to block the use of decision aids in employee selection [W2171321543]. So by the time the modern term appeared, two facts were already established: formulas usually perform better, and people often prefer human judgment anyway.

### 2.2 Algorithm aversion

Early experiments that compared advice sources were run in forecasting. Önkal et al. gave participants identical stock-price forecasts and told them the advice came either from a human expert or from a statistical method. The supposedly statistical advice was discounted much more, even though it improved accuracy either way. The human expert was favored most when both sources were shown side by side [W2158570360]. Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey later coined the term *algorithm aversion*. They showed that people who saw an algorithm make forecasts became less likely to bet on it over an inferior human, even after seeing it win. The reason was that people lost confidence in algorithms faster than in humans after seeing the same mistake [W3125633690]. Later studies confirmed that errors are judged asymmetrically: algorithms that err lose more trust [W2600700815], draw harsher gut reactions and less forgiveness [W3167050492], and gain a bad reputation that fades only slowly over repeated interactions [W4206941179].

Researchers have proposed several mechanisms beyond reactions to errors:
- **Tolerance for error.** People prefer higher-variance human judgment in uncertain domains because it seems more likely to produce a near-perfect answer [W2974452734].
- **Uniqueness neglect.** People doubt that algorithms can account for their particular circumstances [W2942858056].
- **Moral objections.** People object to algorithms that maximize outcomes when moral tradeoffs are involved [W3181173654], and they value human discretion [W4210390504].
- **Implicit prejudice.** An unconscious bias against AI shapes early reliance and fades as people learn how the system performs [W4391114267].

### 2.3 Algorithm appreciation

A second body of work finds the opposite. In six experiments, Logg, Minson and Moore found that people followed advice more when they believed it came from an algorithm rather than a person. They called this *algorithm appreciation* [W2800068874]. Some of their tasks were partly subjective, such as forecasting song popularity and romantic attraction. Appreciation weakened when people weighed the algorithm against their *own* judgment, and among professional forecasters [W2800068874]. Appreciation has been replicated in judge-advisor studies, where it held up even when people were told about the algorithm's errors in summary form [W4281822284]. Reliance on algorithms also rises as intellective tasks get harder [W3152500611]. At the extreme, consumers sometimes over-rely on recommender systems, following algorithmic recommendations even when they are worse, because they believe algorithms have more domain expertise [W4248125493]. Not every study finds aversion. Prahl and Van Swol did not replicate a general preference for human advice [W2600700815]. In public-sector decisions, Alon-Barkat and Busuioc found no automation bias compared with equivalent human-expert advice [W4211002924].

### 2.4 Task type: from forecasting to taste

The type of task is the moderator most relevant to this study. Lee found that for "mechanical" managerial tasks, algorithmic and human decisions were seen as equally fair and trustworthy. For "human" tasks, algorithms were trusted less, because people think they lack intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666]. A recent study of consumers finds both effects within a single design. Algorithms are trusted more on less unstructured tasks, which is mediated by perceived accuracy. Humans are trusted more on highly unstructured tasks, which is mediated by perceived flexibility [W4415545653]. The general advice literature points the same way. A meta-analysis of 129 judge-advisor datasets found that when nothing signaled advice quality, people took more advice on subjective and uncertain estimates than on objective ones [W4292356785]. That makes it important to separate *source* effects from *task* effects.

Taste prediction tests these ideas most directly, because accuracy and perceived suitability come apart there. When predicting which jokes a person will find funny, recommender systems beat strangers, friends and even family. Yet people were reluctant to rely on them, partly because they found human recommendations easier to understand [W2913854599]. For movies, MovieLens collaborative filtering outperformed human recommenders on average, though some individuals and some tasks favored humans [W2075329139]. Together, these studies suggest that aversion in subjective domains is not just a reasonable response to poor algorithm performance. It is a gap between how people *think* algorithms perform and how they actually perform. Several moderators may interact with task type:
- **Difficulty and complexity.** These increase reliance on algorithms [W3152500611], [W3193926864].
- **Lay beliefs about AI.** Believing AI exceeds human intelligence increases reliance, but only on tasks seen as complex [W3193926864].
- **Expertise and self-confidence.** Both reduce reliance [W2800068874], [W3199747482].

### 2.5 Who the human is

Results also depend on how the human comparison is described. Hou and Jung produced both appreciation and aversion just by changing the descriptions of the human and algorithmic agents, with the effect mediated by perceived expertise [W3206874785]. In Önkal et al., the human was explicitly an *expert* [W2158570360]. In Logg et al., it was often an anonymous person or an aggregate of people [W2800068874]. A meta-analysis likewise identifies cues about advice quality as the main driver of how much weight people give advice [W4292356785]. Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl show that whether a study compares algorithm vs. human advisor, algorithm vs. self, or some combination largely determines the direction of the effect [W4400803056]. Reviews call for theory that integrates these factors and point to task-level factors as understudied [W2981686111], [W4200546216].

### 2.6 Interventions and appropriate reliance

Interventions target the proposed mechanisms:
- **Control.** Letting people modify an algorithm's output, even slightly [W3121705224], or choose the training algorithm [W4366547314], increases its use.
- **Learning.** Showing that an algorithm learns from its mistakes reduces aversion [W4283162852], [W3110817755].
- **Understanding.** Making the recommendation process easier to understand may matter more than accuracy in taste domains [W2913854599].

Effects of transparency are mixed. An algorithm that seems too simple loses users [W3189444386], and detailed performance information can reduce appreciation [W4281822284]. Human-factors research reframes the goal as *calibrated* trust rather than as more or less reliance [W4243342770], [W3013998503]. Under that framing, both aversion and overdependence [W4248125493] count as failures.

### 2.7 Gaps addressed by this study

The questions Meehl's critics raised about formulas are now asked about algorithms in domains Meehl never studied, such as humor and entertainment. Yet the evidence on aversion and appreciation is split across studies that differ in **task** (forecasting [W3125633690], [W2158570360] vs. taste [W2913854599]), in **who the human comparison is** (expert vs. layperson [W3206874785]), and in **how reliance is measured** [W4400803056]. Few studies vary task subjectivity within one design while keeping the alternative a human *expert*. [W4415545653] comes close, but it compares agents rather than offering a choice between advice sources. Our study fills this gap by having participants choose between algorithmic and human-expert advice across tasks from forecasting to taste prediction. That lets us test whether the shift from appreciation to aversion follows the perceived subjectivity of the task.

---

### Notes

- **Meehl (1954) isn't in the database.** I described it through the papers that discuss it [W2056418346], [W2102256472], [W2129871510]. Please add the original book to your references. Dawes, Faust & Meehl (1989, *Science*) would also strengthen 2.1.
- **Castelo, Bos & Lehmann (2019, "Task-dependent algorithm aversion")** still didn't turn up. It's probably the closest prior work to your design, because it manipulates perceived task objectivity, so add it to 2.4 and 2.7 by hand. Once it's in, the "few studies" claim in 2.7 needs rechecking.
- **[W4415545653] is from 2025 and has no citations yet.** It's very close to your study, so check it carefully. You'll need to state clearly how your design differs.
- **Check the measurement descriptions.** Many of the studies above measure how much weight people give advice, not a binary choice. Make sure the paper describes your choice measure accurately against those.

### Proposed paragraph (new subsection 2.4, "Reconciling Dietvorst et al. and Logg et al.")

> The two studies most often cited for opposite conclusions are Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey [W3125633690] and Logg, Minson and Moore [W2800068874]. Their findings differ less than their labels suggest. In five studies, Dietvorst et al. had participants see a statistical algorithm make forecasts, see a human make forecasts, see both, or see neither. Participants then decided whether to tie their incentives to the algorithm's or the human's future predictions. Those who had seen the algorithm perform were less confident in it and less likely to choose it over an inferior human forecaster, even if they had seen it outperform the human. The authors attributed this to an asymmetry: people lose confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human after seeing the same mistake [W3125633690]. In a follow-up, people asked to choose between their own forecasts and an imperfect algorithm were much more willing to use it if they could modify its forecasts, even slightly [W3121705224]. Logg et al. measured advice-taking in six experiments rather than a choice of forecaster. Lay participants adjusted their estimates more toward advice they believed came from an algorithm than toward identical advice from a person. This algorithm appreciation held for estimates about a visual stimulus and for forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction. (2) **What the algorithm was compared with.** Logg et al.'s appreciation shrank when the alternative was the participant's own judgment, the comparison used in Dietvorst et al.'s follow-up [W3121705224]. (3) **How reliance was measured.** Dietvorst et al. used an incentivized choice of forecaster, while Logg et al. measured how far people moved toward the advice. Here is the complete section. I merged the earlier drafts into one structure so the history leads into the early studies and then into the Dietvorst/Logg comparison, and each study is described in only one place. A short list of open items follows the section.

---

## 2. Related Work

### 2.1 Origins: clinical versus statistical prediction

Whether to trust formulas or human judgment is a much older question than the term "algorithm aversion." It goes back to Meehl's 1954 book *Clinical versus Statistical Prediction*, which compared expert judgment with formal combinations of the same data [Meehl, 1954]; [W2056418346], [W2129871510]. The roots go back further still. In 1928 Burgess built a parole-outcome predictor from 21 objective factors for about 3,000 Illinois parolees [W2102256472]. Over the following decades, the findings consistently favored the formula. Dawes argued that when a numerical outcome is predicted from numerical inputs, even *improper* linear models beat clinical intuition, including models whose weights are set by intuition or simply made equal [W2056418346]. Grove and Meehl reviewed 136 studies and concluded that the mechanical method is "almost invariably equal to or superior to" the clinical one [W2102256472]. A later meta-analysis put the average advantage at about 10%. Humans were substantially more accurate in only 6–16% of studies, and the result held across tasks, types of judges, and levels of experience [W2168729696]. Machine-learning work points the same way in high-stakes settings such as bail decisions [W2551317447]. In business forecasting, though, combining a model with managerial intuition beat either one on its own [W2104546629]. That suggests "algorithm versus human" is not always the right framing.

This literature also recorded people's **resistance** to formulas from the start. Reviews observed that actuarial methods were rarely used in practice despite being more accurate [W207333959]. Dawes [W2056418346] and Grove and Meehl [W2102256472] discussed the technical, psychological and ethical objections people raise and tried to answer them. Similar beliefs favoring intuition were later shown to block the use of decision aids in employee selection [W2171321543]. So by the time the modern term appeared, two facts were well established: formulas usually perform better, and people often prefer human judgment anyway.

### 2.2 Early experiments comparing advice sources

Experiments that compared a computer source with a human expert, holding the advice constant, predate the label "algorithm aversion." Promberger and Baron found that people were more likely to follow a medical recommendation from a physician than an identical one from a computer program, and trusted the physician more to make a good recommendation [W2070125214]. The preference was partly explained by responsibility. Following any recommendation made people feel less responsible for the outcome, and following a physician reduced that feeling more than following a computer did [W2070125214]. Relatedly, patients rated physicians who used a computerized decision aid lower than physicians who diagnosed unaided. They did not rate physicians lower for consulting an expert colleague. This suggests the penalty is specific to non-human tools rather than to advice-seeking in general [W2085105383]. In forecasting, Önkal et al. gave participants identical stock-price forecasts and told them the advice came either from a human expert or from a statistical method. The supposedly statistical advice was discounted much more, even though it improved accuracy either way. The human expert was favored most when both sources were shown side by side [W2158570360].

### 2.3 Algorithm aversion versus algorithm appreciation: Dietvorst et al. and Logg et al.

The two studies most often cited for opposite conclusions are Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey [W3125633690] and Logg, Minson and Moore [W2800068874]. Their findings differ less than their labels suggest.

In five studies, Dietvorst et al. had participants see a statistical algorithm make forecasts, see a human make forecasts, see both, or see neither. Participants then decided whether to tie their incentives to the algorithm's or the human's future predictions. Those who had seen the algorithm perform were less confident in it and less likely to choose it over an inferior human forecaster, even if they had seen it outperform the human. The authors attributed this to an asymmetry: people lose confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human after seeing the same mistake [W3125633690]. In a follow-up, people asked to choose between their own forecasts and an imperfect algorithm were much more willing to use it if they could modify its forecasts, even slightly. This pointed to a desire for some control over the outcome [W3121705224].

Logg et al. measured advice-taking in six experiments rather than a choice of forecaster. Lay participants adjusted their estimates more toward advice they believed came from an algorithm than toward identical advice from a person. This *algorithm appreciation* held for estimates about a visual stimulus and for forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction. It held whether the advice was presented jointly or separately, and it went against the predictions of surveyed researchers [W2800068874]. Appreciation weakened in two cases: when participants chose between the algorithm's estimate and their *own* rather than another person's, and when participants were experienced professional forecasters. Those professionals relied less on the algorithm, and their accuracy suffered as a result [W2800068874].

The two studies thus differ on at least three dimensions:
1. **What participants knew about performance.** Dietvorst et al.'s aversion appeared specifically after participants had watched the algorithm err.
2. **What the algorithm was compared with.** Logg et al.'s appreciation shrank when the alternative was the participant's own judgment, the comparison used in Dietvorst et al.'s follow-up [W3121705224].
3. **How reliance was measured.** Dietvorst et al. used an incentivized choice of forecaster, while Logg et al. measured how far people moved toward the advice.

Read together, the findings suggest a default willingness to use algorithmic advice that breaks down once people see errors, when the comparison is with themselves, or when the people deciding are experts. This interpretation fits integrative accounts that link the direction of the effect to the decision configuration [W4400803056] and to how the agents are framed [W3206874785].

### 2.4 Further evidence and mechanisms: aversion

Later work supports the idea that algorithmic errors are judged more harshly. After bad advice, people cut their use of automated advice far more than their use of human advice [W2600700815]. Erring algorithms draw harsher gut reactions and less forgiveness than erring humans, and this held regardless of the algorithm's maturity, the severity of the error, or the domain [W3167050492]. In an 18-day field study of financial forecasting, inaccurate algorithms were penalized more than equally inaccurate humans, though the penalty faded over time [W4206941179]. Researchers have also proposed mechanisms beyond reactions to errors:
- **Tolerance for error.** People prefer higher-variance human judgment in uncertain domains because it seems more likely to produce a near-perfect answer [W2974452734].
- **Uniqueness neglect.** People doubt that algorithms can account for their particular circumstances, and resistance to medical AI is stronger among those who see themselves as more unique [W2942858056].
- **Moral objections.** People object to algorithms that maximize outcomes when moral tradeoffs are involved [W3181173654], and they value humans' freedom to depart from fixed fairness rules [W4210390504].
- **Implicit prejudice.** An unconscious bias against AI shapes early reliance, and its weight shrinks as people learn how the system performs [W4391114267].
- **Responsibility.** People may prefer human experts partly because experts absorb responsibility for the outcome [W2070125214].

### 2.5 Further evidence: appreciation and overreliance

Appreciation has been replicated in judge-advisor studies. It was driven by higher trust in the algorithmic advisor and held up even when people were told about the algorithm's errors in summary form [W4281822284]. Reliance on algorithms, relative to the crowd's opinion, also rises as intellective tasks get harder [W3152500611]. At the extreme, consumers sometimes over-rely on recommender systems, following algorithmic recommendations even when they are worse, because they believe algorithms have more domain expertise [W4248125493]. Not every study finds a difference in either direction. Prahl and Van Swol did not replicate a general preference for human advice [W2600700815]. In public-sector decisions, Alon-Barkat and Busuioc found no automation bias compared with equivalent human-expert advice. Instead, both algorithmic and human advice were followed more when it matched stereotypes [W4211002924].

### 2.6 Task type: from forecasting to taste

Lee found that for "mechanical" managerial tasks, algorithmic and human decisions were seen as equally fair and trustworthy. For "human" tasks, algorithms were trusted less, because people think they lack intuition and subjective judgment [W2792183666]. A recent consumer study finds both effects within one design. Algorithms are trusted more on less unstructured tasks, which is mediated by perceived accuracy. Humans are trusted more on highly unstructured tasks, which is mediated by perceived flexibility [W4415545653]. The general advice literature also shows task effects. A meta-analysis of 129 judge-advisor datasets found that when nothing signaled advice quality, people took more advice on subjective and uncertain estimates than on objective ones [W4292356785]. That makes it important to separate *source* effects from *task* effects. [Castelo, Bos & Lehmann, 2019, should be added here.]

Taste prediction tests these ideas most directly, because accuracy and perceived suitability come apart there. When predicting which jokes a person will find funny, recommender systems beat strangers, friends and even family. Yet people were reluctant to rely on them, partly because they found human recommendations easier to understand [W2913854599]. For movies, MovieLens collaborative filtering outperformed human recommenders on average, though some individuals and some tasks favored humans [W2075329139]. Together, these studies suggest that aversion in subjective domains reflects a gap between how people think algorithms perform and how they actually perform, not a reasonable response to poor algorithm performance. Several moderators may interact with task type:
- **Difficulty and complexity.** These increase reliance on algorithms [W3152500611], [W3193926864].
- **Lay beliefs about AI.** Believing AI exceeds human intelligence increases reliance, but only on tasks seen as complex [W3193926864].
- **Expertise and self-confidence.** Both reduce reliance [W2800068874], [W3199747482].

### 2.7 Who the human is, and how reliance is measured

Results also depend on how the human comparison is described. Hou and Jung produced both appreciation and aversion just by changing the descriptions of the human and algorithmic agents, with the effect mediated by perceived expertise [W3206874785]. Studies that framed the human as an expert, such as a physician [W2070125214] or a forecasting expert [W2158570360], tended to find a preference for the human. Logg et al.'s appreciation results often compared the algorithm with non-expert people [W2800068874]. Across judge-advisor studies, cues about advice quality are the main driver of how much weight advice receives [W4292356785]. Measurement matters as well. Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl show that whether a study compares algorithm vs. human advisor, algorithm vs. self, or some combination largely determines the direction of the effect. They also note that the field lacks shared definitions and measures [W4400803056]. Systematic reviews call for theory that integrates these factors [W2981686111] and point to task-level factors as understudied compared with features of the algorithm and the individual [W4200546216].

### 2.8 Interventions and appropriate reliance

Interventions target the proposed mechanisms:
- **Control.** Letting people modify an algorithm's output increases its use [W3121705224]. A replication only partly confirmed this effect, and found that letting people choose the training algorithm also helps [W4366547314].
- **Learning.** Showing that an algorithm learns from its mistakes reduces aversion [W4283162852], [W3110817755].
- **Personalization and support roles.** In medicine, framing AI as personalized, or as supporting rather than replacing a clinician, removes resistance [W2942858056].
- **Understanding.** Making the recommendation process easier to understand may matter more than accuracy in taste domains [W2913854599].

Effects of transparency are mixed. An algorithm that seems too simple loses users [W3189444386], and detailed performance information can reduce appreciation by increasing cognitive load [W4281822284]. Human-factors research reframes the goal as *calibrated* trust rather than more or less reliance [W4243342770]. Reviews of trust in AI separate cognitive trust from emotional trust and note that the evidence relies heavily on short-term lab studies [W3013998503]. Under this framing, both aversion and overdependence [W4248125493] count as failures, as does continuing to rely on a poor AI because people blame themselves for its errors [W3199747482].

### 2.9 Gaps addressed by this study

The questions Meehl's critics raised about formulas are now asked about algorithms in domains Meehl never studied, such as humor and entertainment. Yet the evidence on aversion and appreciation is split across studies that differ in three ways:
- **Task:** medical [W2070125214], forecasting [W3125633690], [W2158570360], [W2800068874], or taste [W2913854599], [W2075329139].
- **Who the human comparison is:** expert, layperson, or the self [W3206874785], [W4400803056].
- **How reliance is measured:** choice [W3125633690] or advice weighting [W2800068874].

The two studies this design builds on most directly did not vary how subjective the task was within one design. Logg et al.'s song and romance tasks are the closest, and those still had objectively scorable answers [W2800068874]. Few studies vary task subjectivity while keeping the alternative a human *expert*. [W4415545653] comes close, but it compares trust in agents rather than offering a choice between advice sources. Our study fills this gap by having participants choose between algorithmic and human-expert advice across tasks from forecasting to taste prediction. That lets us test whether the shift from appreciation to aversion follows the perceived subjectivity of the task.

---

### Open items before submission

1. **Citations to add by hand.** Meehl (1954) and Castelo, Bos & Lehmann (2019) aren't in the database, so they appear as bracketed placeholders. Castelo et al. manipulates perceived task objectivity, so once it's in, recheck the "few studies" claim in 2.9. Dawes, Faust & Meehl (1989, *Science*) would also strengthen 2.1.
2. **Checks against the full papers.** I worked from abstracts only, so verify four things:
   - That Logg et al.'s participants saw no performance feedback (contrast 1 in 2.3).
   - Who the "human forecaster" was in each Dietvorst et al. study (contrast 2).
   - That Logg et al.'s human advisors were non-experts (2.7).
   - The specific tasks and sample sizes, if reviewers will expect them.
3. **Reference years.** The database lists Dietvorst et al.'s aversion paper as 2014, but it appeared in *JEP: General* in 2015. Logg et al. should be cited as *OBHDP* 2019, not the 2017 SSRN preprint.
